## MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.

### SUMMARY

### Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures

Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. **Fiscal Impact:** Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. **Supporters:** California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing **Opponents:** Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation

### WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS

YES A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.

NO A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.

CON PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. ## PROP  
 45

## MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.

## ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST

### BACKGROUND

***State Law Requires Government Agencies to Review the Environmental Impacts of Proposed Projects.*** State and local government agencies are responsible for reviewing and approving certain projects before they can be built. As part of this process, the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires an agency to consider how a project might negatively affect the environment before approving it. CEQA applies to many types of public and private projects, such as housing developments, school facilities, and highway expansions. Some exceptions apply. For example, state law exempts certain housing developments located near public transit from needing a CEQA review.

***How the CEQA Process Works.*** The government agency first determines if CEQA applies to a project. If so, it then determines if the project could significantly affect the environment and if those impacts could be avoided or reduced with minor changes to the project. If making minor changes cannot avoid or reduce significant impacts, the agency must do a more detailed review called an environmental impact report (EIR). (The majority of projects do not require an EIR; however, EIRs are somewhat more common for large and complex projects.) The EIR analyzes possible environmental impacts the project could cause and considers alternatives that could reduce those impacts. After finishing the environmental review, the agency decides whether to approve the project. At certain times during this process, the government agency must seek and consider comments about the project’s environmental review from the public and other government agencies.

***People Can Sue the Government Agency About Its CEQA Review.*** After a government agency has completed the CEQA review and decided whether to approve a project, people who think the agency did not follow the CEQA process correctly can sue the agency. For example, a project opponent might argue that the environmental analysis was inadequate. If the court finds that the agency did not follow CEQA correctly, it can stop the whole project and require the agency to fix the part of the process that was problematic.

***Many Projects Also Need to Get Other Approvals.*** Besides CEQA review, many projects need approval or permits from other local and/or state government agencies before they can proceed. For example, a business that wants to build a health clinic might need the local government to change land use rules before it can proceed. It also may need state agencies to review and approve how the project might affect certain wildlife species and water quality.

### PROPOSAL

Proposition 45 creates new procedures for reviewing certain types of projects that it defines as “essential.” Figure 1 lists the types of projects eligible for the new procedures. The proposition (1) tightens time limits for CEQA review, permits, and court challenges; (2) changes parts of the CEQA review process; and (3) changes the court’s review process for CEQA lawsuits. The proposition gives eligible project applicants the option of using the new procedures or existing procedures.

![Types of Projects Eligible to Use Proposition 45’s New Procedures • Housing. • Water system (not including Delta conveyance facilities). • Clean energy (not including nuclear power). • Health facility, clinic, and medical office building. • Fire, police, and sheriff’s stations. • Wildfire risk reduction. • Broadband Internet access. • Education facility. • Transportation (not including high-speed rail).](/img/45/prop-45-fig-1.jpg)

 

***Tightens Time Limits for Review and Court Challenges of Eligible Projects.*** Proposition 45 creates more binding time limits for state and local governments to do both CEQA and permitting reviews. This includes time limits for determining if a project application is complete, finishing the EIR, and granting other types of approvals and permits. For example, Proposition 45 allows an applicant to request an agency hearing— and potentially file a lawsuit with the courts—if an agency does not meet the 365-business-day time limit for finishing the EIR. The proposition also creates a time limit for courts to resolve legal challenges.

***Changes CEQA Review for Eligible Projects.*** For eligible projects, Proposition 45 makes several changes to the CEQA review process, including: 

*   ***Application Process.*** Requires the government agency to specify all information that must be included in an application before it is submitted. (Current law allows agencies to repeatedly request additional information or project changes.)
*   ***How Environmental Impacts Are Assessed.*** Requires the agency to assess potential environmental impacts based on the laws and standards in place at the time the project application is submitted. (Current law lets the agency consider new information and revise its review standards when doing the EIR.)
*   ***Project Alternatives.*** Allows the applicant to develop only one project alternative for the agency to consider. (Current law requires the agency—not the applicant—to develop and consider multiple project alternatives that could reduce environmental impacts.)
*   ***Consultation With Native Tribes.*** Requires the agency and applicant to consult about the project only with California native tribes that have been formally recognized by the federal government. (Current law requires consultation with a wider range of tribes.)
*   ***Public Comment Periods.*** Limits how long the agency can accept comments from the public and other government agencies about the project. (Current law sets a minimum number of days—not a maximum—for public review.)

***Changes How Courts Review Challenges to Eligible Projects.*** Proposition 45 makes several changes to the court’s review process when someone challenges a government agency’s approval of an eligible project. For example, it reduces the scope of what the court can consider in CEQA lawsuits. The proposition also prevents the court from stopping the whole project if it finds that the agency did not follow CEQA correctly. Instead, the court can only stop the part of the project where the environmental review did not comply with CEQA while the agency fixes the problem.

### FISCAL EFFECTS

***Initial Costs for State and Local Governments.*** During the first several years, Proposition 45 likely would increase costs for the state and local governments, including state courts. These costs likely would be in the **high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially exceeding $100 million annually**. For example, state and local governments would have costs to develop new guidelines and standards for reviewing eligible projects’ environmental impacts, meet tighter time limits, and address court challenges. Fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits would cover some of these costs. After this initial period, while some costs could continue, others likely would decline over time. For example, the changes to how courts can review CEQA lawsuits could mean fewer people will sue in the future, which could reduce costs for agencies and state courts in the long term.

***In the Longer Term, Uncertain but Potentially More Significant Fiscal Effects.*** Proposition 45’s changes to project review and court challenge procedures for eligible projects could have various fiscal effects for state and local governments. The overall fiscal effect of these changes—positive or negative—is uncertain but could be more substantial than the near-term effects. For example, two effects that could have significant but uncertain impacts are: 

*   ***More Projects and Faster Timing.*** To the degree that Proposition 45’s changes to project review and court challenge procedures lead to eligible public projects being constructed more quickly, state and local governments likely would have lower project costs. Additionally, if the proposition’s changes result in more projects being completed overall, it could lead to an increase in tax revenues, such as from property taxes.
*   ***Negative Environmental Impacts.*** To the degree that Proposition 45’s changes to project review and court challenge procedures lead to approval of projects with negative environmental impacts that would not have otherwise occurred, government agencies could face higher costs to respond to those impacts.

## MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.

### ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 45

LENGTHY DELAYS AND RED TAPE ARE BLOCKING ESSENTIAL PROJECTS & DRIVING UP OUR COST OF LIVING.

Families cannot afford to live in California because we are failing to deliver the basics. California’s outdated system for approving essential housing, water, clean energy, roads, schools, hospitals, and wildfire prevention projects is too slow, too bureaucratic, and too costly—driving up the cost of living for everyone.

Endless delays, red tape, and frivolous lawsuits make life more expensive and block the projects Californians need—driving up costs for housing, electricity, and water; wasting taxpayer dollars; worsening wildfire risk; increasing traffic; overcrowding schools; and delaying hospital and infrastructure upgrades.

PROP. 45 *LOWERS OUR HIGH COST OF LIVING* BY MAKING IT FASTER & LESS EXPENSIVE TO BUILD ESSENTIAL PROJECTS.

Prop. 45 streamlines approvals by setting enforceable timelines for project approvals; requires courts and government agencies to base decisions on the laws and regulations in place when the project application is submitted; and creates a faster, more predictable process for legal challenges while reducing frivolous lawsuits.

PROP. 45 STREAMLINES CALIFORNIA’S MOST-PRESSING ESSENTIAL PROJECTS, INCLUDING:

• Water quality and supply projects • Hospitals and healthcare facilities • Housing, including homes and apartments • Wildfire prevention • Schools and classrooms • Roads, bridges and transit • Clean energy and electric grid reliability infrastructure

PROP. 45 WILL: 

*   REDUCE THE COST OF HOUSING. Permitting delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new home. Prop. 45 will help lower rents and mortgages and save families tens of thousands of dollars on a home purchase.
*   LOWER ELECTRICITY COSTS. Delays in building clean energy and electric grid infrastructure drive up electricity costs for working families. Prop. 45 helps lower electricity costs.
*   PROTECT TAXPAYERS. Lengthy delays drive massive cost overruns on public projects—roads, schools, hospitals, water systems, and wildfire prevention—costing taxpayers billions more. Prop. 45 cuts costly delays, reduces costs, and helps keep projects on time and on budget.
*   CREATE GOOD-PAYING JOBS AND STRENGTHEN OUR ECONOMY. Prop. 45 will create tens of thousands of good-paying jobs and billions in economic activity.

PROP. 45 MAINTAINS CALIFORNIA’S STRONGEST-IN-THE-NATION ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTIONS.

California should not have to choose between protecting the environment and building the essential projects we need. Under Prop. 45, projects must comply with *all* of California strong environmental laws protecting our air, water, wildlife, and health. Prop. 45 *does not* exempt a single project from environmental review.

PROP. 45 PROTECTS COMMUNITY INPUT AND LOCAL DECISION MAKING.

Under Prop. 45, cities and counties retain full authority to approve or deny projects, and residents keep a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their communities.

AFFORDABLE HOUSING ADVOCATES, HEALTHCARE PROFESSIONALS, EDUCATORS, WATER PROVIDERS, CLEAN ENERGY LEADERS AND CIVIL RIGHTS LEADERS SUPPORT PROP. 45.

Prop. 45 is supported by a broad coalition of organizations, including:

• American Clean Power—California • California League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC) • NAACP California/Hawaii State Conference • California Taxpayers Association • Environmental Policy Innovation Center

YES ON PROP. 45 TO BUILD A MORE AFFORDABLE CALIFORNIA.

Every year of delay means Californians *wait longer* and *pay more* for the essential projects we need. It’s time to cut red tape, protect our environment and build the projects California needs to make life more affordable.

VOTE YES ON PROP. 45.

*YESonProp45.com*

**Ann-Louise Kuhns**, President  
 California Children’s Hospital Association  
 **Jennifer Capitolo**, Executive Director  
 California Water Association  
 **Jenna Abbott**, Executive Director  
 California Council on Affordable Housing

### REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 45

PROPOSITION 45 WON’T LOWER YOUR COSTS.

It doesn’t require a single project to lower your rent, your mortgage, or your utility bills. 45’s corporate funders profit while you bear the cost of their pollution.

PROP. 45 DOESN’T DELIVER AN AFFORDABLE CALIFORNIA. IT LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW AND RISKS PUBLIC HEALTH.

Prop. 45 could have been about building what California needs. It isn’t. Funded by gas and electric utilities and corporate PACs, Prop. 45 cuts their costs, not yours. Prop. 45 flips California law to protect their projects, harming public health and our air and water.

PROP. 45 PUTS YOUR HEALTH AT RISK AND STICKS YOU WITH THE BILL. Weaker environmental review means more pollution near homes and schools, more asthma and more emergency-room visits. When polluters don’t clean up, taxpayers and ratepayers pay more to cover the costs.

PROP. 45 TAKES AWAY PUBLIC INPUT. It limits the environmental review of new projects and your right to provide input and be heard. 45 even gives developers new rights to challenge cities and counties, while making it more difficult for project opponents to successfully challenge an agency’s decision.

Prop. 45 rewrites the rules that govern how California protects its citizens from the harm caused by major developments. Prop. 45 weakens environmental safeguards and radically shifts power to corporate polluters.

Protect your air quality, your drinking water, your family’s health, your tax dollars, and your right to be heard.

Join nurses, community and public health advocates.

VOTE NO ON PROP. 45.

*www.NoProp45CA.com*

**Chris Tarver**, R.N., President  
 American Nurses Association, CA  
 **Vanessa Forsythe**, RN  
 California Nurses for Environmental Health and Justice  
 **Martha Arguello**, Executive Director  
 Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA

# **Proposition 45**

Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.

* * *

## Analysis of Measure

### Background

***State Law Requires Government Agencies to Review the Environmental Impacts of Proposed Projects.*** State and local government agencies are responsible for reviewing and approving certain projects before they can be built. As part of this process, the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires an agency to consider how a project might negatively affect the environment before approving it. CEQA applies to many types of public and private projects, such as housing developments, school facilities, and highway expansions. Some exceptions apply. For example, state law exempts certain housing developments located near public transit from needing a CEQA review.

***How the CEQA Process Works.*** The government agency first determines if CEQA applies to a project. If so, it then determines if the project could significantly affect the environment and if those impacts could be avoided or reduced with minor changes to the project. If making minor changes cannot avoid or reduce significant impacts, the agency must do a more detailed review called an environmental impact report (EIR). (The majority of projects do not require an EIR; however, EIRs are somewhat more common for large and complex projects.) The EIR analyzes possible environmental impacts the project could cause and considers alternatives that could reduce those impacts. After finishing the environmental review, the agency decides whether to approve the project. At certain times during this process, the government agency must seek and consider comments about the project’s environmental review from the public and other government agencies.

***People Can Sue the Government Agency About Its CEQA Review.*** After a government agency has completed the CEQA review and decided whether to approve a project, people who think the agency did not follow the CEQA process correctly can sue the agency. For example, a project opponent might argue that the environmental analysis was inadequate. If the court finds that the agency did not follow CEQA correctly, it can stop the whole project and require the agency to fix the part of the process that was problematic.

***Many Projects Also Need to Get Other Approvals.*** Besides CEQA review, many projects need approval or permits from other local and/or state government agencies before they can proceed. For example, a business that wants to build a health clinic might need the local government to change land use rules before it can proceed. It also may need state agencies to review and approve how the project might affect certain wildlife species and water quality.

### Proposal

Proposition 45 creates new procedures for reviewing certain types of projects that it defines as “essential.” Figure 1 lists the types of projects eligible for the new procedures. The proposition (1) tightens time limits for CEQA review, permits, and court challenges; (2) changes parts of the CEQA review process; and (3) changes the court’s review process for CEQA lawsuits. The proposition gives eligible project applicants the option of using the new procedures or existing procedures.

![Figure 1: Types of Projects Eligible to Use Proposition 45's New Procedures](/ballot/2026/prop45-fig1.png)

***Tightens Time Limits for Review and Court Challenges of Eligible Projects.*** Proposition 45 creates more binding time limits for state and local governments to do both CEQA and permitting reviews. This includes time limits for determining if a project application is complete, finishing the EIR, and granting other types of approvals and permits. For example, Proposition 45 allows an applicant to request an agency hearing—and potentially file a lawsuit with the courts—if an agency does not meet the 365-business-day time limit for finishing the EIR. The proposition also creates a time limit for courts to resolve legal challenges.

***Changes CEQA Review for Eligible Projects.*** For eligible projects, Proposition 45 makes several changes to the CEQA review process, including:

*   ***Application Process.*** Requires the government agency to specify all information that must be included in an application before it is submitted. (Current law allows agencies to repeatedly request additional information or project changes.)
*   ***How Environmental Impacts Are Assessed.*** Requires the agency to assess potential environmental impacts based on the laws and standards in place at the time the project application is submitted. (Current law lets the agency consider new information and revise its review standards when doing the EIR.)
*   ***Project Alternatives.*** Allows the applicant to develop only one project alternative for the agency to consider. (Current law requires the agency—not the applicant—to develop and consider multiple project alternatives that could reduce environmental impacts.)
*   ***Consultation With Native Tribes.*** Requires the agency and applicant to consult about the project only with California native tribes that have been formally recognized by the federal government. (Current law requires consultation with a wider range of tribes.)
*   ***Public Comment Periods.*** Limits how long the agency can accept comments from the public and other government agencies about the project. (Current law sets a minimum number of days—not a maximum—for public review.)

***Changes How Courts Review Challenges to Eligible Projects.*** Proposition 45 makes several changes to the court’s review process when someone challenges a government agency’s approval of an eligible project. For example, it reduces the scope of what the court can consider in CEQA lawsuits. The proposition also prevents the court from stopping the whole project if it finds that the agency did not follow CEQA correctly. Instead, the court can only stop the part of the project where the environmental review did not comply with CEQA while the agency fixes the problem.

### Fiscal Effects

***Initial Costs for State and Local Governments.*** During the first several years, Proposition 45 likely would increase costs for the state and local governments, including state courts. These costs likely would be in the **high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially exceeding $100 million annually**. For example, state and local governments would have costs to develop new guidelines and standards for reviewing eligible projects’ environmental impacts, meet tighter time limits, and address court challenges. Fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits would cover some of these costs. After this initial period, while some costs could continue, others likely would decline over time. For example, the changes to how courts can review CEQA lawsuits could mean fewer people will sue in the future, which could reduce costs for agencies and state courts in the long term.

***In the Longer Term, Uncertain but Potentially More Significant Fiscal Effects.*** Proposition 45’s changes to project review and court challenge procedures for eligible projects could have various fiscal effects for state and local governments. The overall fiscal effect of these changes—positive or negative—is uncertain but could be more substantial than the near-term effects. For example, two effects that could have significant but uncertain impacts are:

*   ***More Projects and Faster Timing.*** To the degree that Proposition 45’s changes to project review and court challenge procedures lead to eligible public projects being constructed more quickly, state and local governments likely would have lower project costs. Additionally, if the proposition’s changes result in more projects being completed overall, it could lead to an increase in tax revenues, such as from property taxes.
*   ***Negative Environmental Impacts.*** To the degree that Proposition 45’s changes to project review and court challenge procedures lead to approval of projects with negative environmental impacts that would not have otherwise occurred, government agencies could face higher costs to respond to those impacts.

* * *

## Yes/No Statement

A **YES** vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.

A **NO** vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.

* * *

## Summary of Legislative Analyst’s Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact

*   Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars annually—potentially exceeding $100 million annually—to implement new project review and court challenge procedures for eligible projects. Fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits would partly cover these costs.
*   In the longer term, uncertain, but potentially more significant positive or negative fiscal effects for state and local governments. The overall effect depends, in part, on how the new procedures change the number of eligible projects that get built and whether those projects have different environmental impacts.

* * *

## Ballot Label

**Fiscal Impact**: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects.

# PROP 45: The CEQA “Essential Projects” Fast Track (Building an Affordable California Act)

[Download PDF](<https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California Decides_Proposition 45.pdf>)

###### Quick Facts

*   **Official ballot title:** “Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney General title and summary, December 26, 2025)
*   **Measure’s own name:** The Building an Affordable California Act (AG No. 25-0023A1)
*   **Type:** Initiated state statute
*   **A vote YES means:** A new “essential projects” category (most housing, water, clean energy, medical, public safety, broadband, and transportation projects) gets hard deadlines for CEQA review, a slimmed-down alternatives analysis, and tighter limits on lawsuits, all written into the Public Resources Code \[1, Sec. 21013\].
*   **A vote NO means:** CEQA’s existing review timelines, alternatives requirements, and judicial-review rules stay in place for these projects.
*   **Sponsor/proponent:** California Chamber of Commerce. Proponent of record: Kurt R. Oneto of Nielsen Merksamer LLP.
*   **On the ballot because:** Qualified by random-sample signature check on June 16, 2026, and certified eligible June 25, 2026. The measure needed 546,651 valid signatures.
*   **Full legal text:** [Initiative 25-0023A1, “Building an Affordable California Act,” Office of the Attorney General (PDF)](https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf)
*   **LAO analysis:** [Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0023](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-023)

###### 1\. What would it do?

Proposition 45 would carve a new fast-track lane through the California Environmental Quality Act for what it calls “essential projects.” It adds a new chapter, Chapter 1.5, to Division 13 of the Public Resources Code, the part of state law that is CEQA. It does not repeal CEQA, and it does not touch the other environmental statutes it names, such as the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the California Coastal Act. What it changes is CEQA’s procedure for a defined set of projects \[1, Sec. 1 (21011(h)), 21012-21033\].

The measure does three main things for essential projects. First, it puts public agencies on a clock. An agency has thirty days to decide whether an application is complete or the application is deemed complete automatically. Once complete, a lead agency has 365 days to decide whether to certify an environmental impact report (EIR), 180 days to act on a negative declaration, and 90 days to document an exemption. For the 365-day and 90-day review clocks the measure counts only business days, not weekends or state holidays, so the real-world calendar is longer than the raw numbers suggest \[1, Secs. 21017-21019, 21028(c)\].

Second, it shrinks the alternatives analysis. Today a CEQA environmental impact report must study a reasonable range of alternatives to a project. Under Proposition 45, an EIR for an essential project needs to analyze only the project itself, one alternative developed by the applicant, and the “no project” alternative. The measure declares that any additional alternatives are “unnecessary” and that no agency may require them \[1, Sec. 21025\].

Third, it narrows the courtroom. A challenger must sue within thirty days of the agency’s notice of determination, the case must finish within 270 days including any appeal, and the court must use the deferential substantial-evidence standard rather than independent judgment. A court that finds a defect may order the agency to redo only the specific study at issue. It “may not order or direct” the agency to rescind its approval of the project, and once a project clears review its later construction and implementation approvals cannot be challenged again \[1, Secs. 21026-21027\].

 

###### 2\. The legal language

*   **Full text:** [Initiative 25-0023A1, “Building an Affordable California Act,” California Office of the Attorney General](https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (amended language submitted November 24, 2025)
*   **Key language:**

“‘Essential project’ means a project that meets all of the following requirements … The project does not include a jail or other detention facility, or involve the development of a new oil or natural gas production facility.” \[1, Sec. 21028(h)\]

“A court may not order or direct via writ or any other form of order, injunction, or decision that an agency rescind its approval of the essential project.” \[1, Sec. 21027(d)\]

*   **What it amends:** Adds Chapter 1.5 (commencing with Section 21010) to Division 13 of the Public Resources Code. Because it is an initiative statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, but only in ways that further the measure’s purposes unless it says otherwise. The measure also adds a self-defense clause. If the governor and attorney general both decline to defend it in court, the attorney general must appoint independent counsel, funded by a continuous general fund appropriation \[1, Secs. 21010, Section 4\].

 

###### 3\. What, Where, When, Why?

*   **Who?** Sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, with the initiative filed by attorney Kurt R. Oneto of Nielsen Merksamer. Supporters include the California Building Industry Association, the California Hospital Association, NAACP California, and Pacific Gas and Electric. Opposition is led by environmental organizations, including Sierra Club California, the Planning and Conservation League, and CalBike.
*   **What?** A new “essential projects” category covering most housing, water, clean energy, medical, public-safety, broadband, and transportation projects, given fixed review deadlines, a one-alternative EIR, and tighter judicial review. Jails and detention facilities and new oil and gas production facilities are excluded, and by definition Delta conveyance and high-speed rail are left out of the water and transportation categories. \[1, Secs. 21013, 21028\].
*   **Where?** Statewide, applied to all public agencies and written into the Public Resources Code \[1, Sec. 21014(d)\].
*   **When?** On the November 3, 2026, ballot. It takes effect the day after the election if it passes and applies to applications deemed complete after that date, including projects that withdraw and resubmit to opt in \[1, Secs. 21014(f)-(g), 21033\].
*   **Why?** The proponents frame CEQA delay and litigation as a driver of California’s high housing, energy, and infrastructure costs. Their stated purpose is to “make California more affordable by streamlining and speeding up approval of essential projects” while keeping the state’s other environmental laws intact \[1, Secs. 21011-21012\].

###### 4\. Trade-offs

CEQA review and the lawsuits that follow can add years and cost to housing and infrastructure, and the delay is not evenly aimed at the most polluting projects. The legislature itself has spent recent sessions passing narrower CEQA exemptions for infill housing and other priorities, which shows that the cost-of-building concern is bipartisan and real, not manufactured. Proposition 45 is the broadest response yet because it does by initiative, and across seven whole project categories, what the legislature has done piecemeal.

Every lever the measure pulls to go faster also removes a check that CEQA built in on purpose. Hard deadlines with a “deemed complete” default speed things up, and they also let a clock, rather than a finished analysis, decide when review ends. A one-alternative EIR is cheaper and quicker, and it also means the public document may never study the option that would have reduced harm the most. The substantial-evidence standard and the bar on rescinding approvals cut litigation risk for builders, and they also make it harder for a neighbor or a tribe to stop a project that was genuinely under-analyzed. None of these is a free lunch. Each is a real gain in speed bought with a real reduction in review.

Two things keep this from being a simple pro-building versus pro-environment fight. First, the measure leaves the substantive environmental statutes standing. A project that violates the Clean Water Act or the Endangered Species Act is still illegal under those laws. What changes is CEQA’s procedural review, which is disclosure and analysis, not the pollution limits themselves. Second, the fight will be about the word “essential.” The definitions are broad. “Essential clean energy” reaches carbon-capture and hydrogen infrastructure, and the categories sweep in “related and ancillary” infrastructure as part of the “whole of the project.” How wide that lane runs, and how much of California’s building actually qualifies, is the question the ballot label cannot answer \[1, Secs. 21028(f), (h)\].

Many CEQA issues are not about acceptable levels of environmental damage. Instead, project opponents use procedural complaints under CEQA to slow down projects that they dislike for reasons having nothing to do with the environment. The proposition’s backers wish to reduce the use of CEQA for such purposes.

## 5\. Potential risks and benefits

**Potential benefits**

*   It replaces open-ended CEQA timelines with firm deadlines, which can cut the years of delay that raise the cost of housing, water, clean energy, and hospitals \[1, Secs. 21018-21019\].
*   The streamlined one-alternative EIR reduces the cost and length of environmental review while still requiring a “no project” comparison \[1, Sec. 21025\].
*   Tighter judicial rules, a 270-day case clock, and a bar on rescinding approvals reduce the litigation risk that can stall financing on approved projects \[1, Secs. 21026-21027\].
*   The LAO expects state and local governments to see long-run net savings from reduced administrative and legal workload once the system is running.
*   It leaves the underlying pollution-control statutes—the Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, Endangered Species Act, and Coastal Act—in force, so it narrows CEQA procedure rather than repealing environmental protection \[1, Sec. 21011(h)\].

**Potential risks**

*   A one-alternative EIR and a “deemed complete” default can end review before the analysis is finished, so real environmental or community harms may go unstudied \[1, Secs. 21017, 21025\].
*   The bar on rescinding an approval and on challenging later construction approvals sharply limits the public’s ability to stop an under-reviewed project \[1, Sec. 21027(d)-(e)\].
*   The “essential project” definitions are broad and include ancillary infrastructure, so fights over what qualifies will be frequent and consequential \[1, Sec. 21028(h)\].
*   The LAO estimates implementation costs in the tens of millions of dollars annually for the first several years, with uncertain long-run court effects that could run from savings to added costs.
*   The self-defense clause commits an open-ended general fund appropriation to hired outside counsel if state officials decline to defend the measure \[1, Section 4\].

## 6\. Open questions

*   How much of California’s actual building pipeline meets the “essential project” definition once ancillary infrastructure and the seven categories are counted?

*   Will the 365 business-day and 90 business-day clocks, which run longer than calendar deadlines, deliver the speed proponents promise?
*   Does limiting an EIR to one applicant-designed alternative meaningfully weaken the document’s ability to surface lower-impact options?
*   How will courts read “objective, quantifiable, and written standards” as the new test for a valid CEQA challenge, and how many suits does that screen out?
*   If the measure passes, how much litigation will target the boundaries of the definitions themselves, and who pays for the state’s defense under the independent-counsel clause?

###### 7\. The questions to ask before you vote

CEQA delay is a real driver of what it costs to build housing, water projects, and energy capacity in California. Proposition 45 speeds up those projects by shortening deadlines, shrinking the alternatives study, and limiting lawsuits. The questions are whether faster building is worth a lighter environmental and public review and whether to trust the broad definition of “essential” to stay in its lane.

Every provision that makes a project go faster also removes a check that CEQA put there on purpose. Which risk weighs more: a needed project stalled for years by process and litigation or a harmful project approved before the harm was fully studied?

 **California Proposition 45**, the **Expedited Environmental Review Process for Certain Projects Initiative**, is on the [ballot](/California_2026_ballot_propositions "California 2026 ballot propositions") in [California](/California "California") as an [initiated state statute](/Initiated_state_statute "Initiated state statute") on [November 3, 2026](/California_2026_ballot_propositions "California 2026 ballot propositions").[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

A "**yes**" vote supports this initiative to make changes to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to:

*   establish deadlines for public agencies to complete environmental review and take required actions for projects deemed *essential* under the law;
*   limit public agencies' existing requirement to consider a range of project alternatives to reduce environmental impacts; and
*   change the court review process for project approvals by setting deadlines for filing and resolving lawsuits and limiting the evidence and relief the court can consider and order.

A "**no**" vote opposes this initiative to make changes to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), which governs state and local government agencies' review process for determining potential environmental impacts and mitigation solutions of proposed construction projects.

## Overview

### How would the initiative change the timelines for California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and Permit Streamlining Act (PSA) reviews?

*See also: [Measure design](#Measure_design)*

The initiative would amend the [California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)](#California_Environmental_Quality_Act_\(CEQA\)) and the [Permit Streamlining Act](#Permit_Streamlining_Act) by shortening the review process for a defined set of essential projects — housing, water systems (excluding Delta conveyance), clean energy, medical facilities, public safety infrastructure (excluding jails/prisons), broadband, education, and transportation (excluding high-speed rail).[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

Agencies would have 30 days to determine whether an application is complete, covering environmental review, permitting, and court proceedings. If no determination is made within that window, the application is automatically deemed complete. This would apply even when local general plan or zoning changes are required. The 30-day rule would apply to both lead agencies (the agency principally responsible for approving the project) and responsible agencies (other public agencies with a role in approval).[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

The initiative would shift environmental review and permitting timelines from calendar days to business days and require lead agencies to issue permit decisions at the same time as the environmental review, rather than after. If agencies miss deadlines, applicants can grant more time to the agency or request a hearing. The initiative would also authorize applicants to challenge adverse decisions in court and require that such challenges be resolved within 270 days (with a possible 90-day extension).[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

### How would the initiative change the environmental review process?

*See also: [Measure design](#Measure_design)*

The initiative would limit public comment periods for essential project environmental impact reports (EIRs) to 45 days. Currently, state law sets a minimum rather than a maximum. It would require a court order to extend that window. It would also establish an optional preliminary scoping process in which applicants meet with the lead agency to discuss the project and potential impacts, after which the applicant may develop a single alternative for EIR consideration. Currently, state law requires agencies to develop and evaluate a range of alternatives. Additionally, agencies would be required to base their environmental impact evaluations on existing laws and the significance thresholds in place at the time of application, rather than applying varying or project-specific thresholds as currently permitted.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

The EIR process also includes a tribal consultation component. The initiative would require applicants and lead agencies to consult with native tribes listed as federally recognized, not the state Native American Heritage Commission list. It would also require applicants to be screened by the lead agency and by tribes that may be affected by the project's impacts on their cultural resources. A good-faith tribal consultation would also be a prerequisite for lead agency approval.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

### Who supports and opposes the initiative?

*See also: [Support](#Support) and [Opposition](#Opposition)*

[Committee to Build an Affordable California](#Support) is leading the Yes on Prop 45 campaign. We can protect the environment and good-paying jobs while delivering the essential projects California urgently needs."[\[2\]](#cite_note-support-2)[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)

Essential projects definition

The initiative would make changes to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and Permit Streamlining Act (PSA) as it relates to essential projects. Essential projects would include the following list of projects and associated infrastructure:

*   housing,
*   water systems (excluding Delta conveyance facilities),
*   clean energy,
*   medical treatment facilities,
*   public safety (including first responder facilities and wildfire risk reduction; excluding jails or prisons),
*   broadband internet access,
*   education facilities, and
*   transportation (excluding high-speed rail).

  
 

Essential project applicants using the process proposed by the initiative would also be subject to certain labor requirements. The initiative would allow applicants who submitted applications prior to the implementation of the initiative to withdraw their applications and resubmit according to the new process.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)[\[5\]](#cite_note-lao-5)

Changes to CEQA and PSA time limits

The initiative would set a 30-day time limit for lead or responsible agencies to determine whether an essential project application is complete. This would apply to projects needing local general plan or zoning changes. If the lead or responsible agency does not make a determination within 30 days, the application is automatically considered complete. A lead agency is defined in CEQA as "public agency which has the principal responsibility for carrying out or approving a project." A responsible agency is a "public agency which proposes to carry out or approve a project, for which a lead agency is preparing or has prepared an EIR or negative declaration."[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

  
 The initiative would change environmental review timelines by using business days instead of calendar days. It would extend the time limit from 90 calendar days to 90 business days for lead agencies to determine if the project is exempt from an environmental review. If the agency does not meet the established time limit, the applicant may either grant the agency more time or request a meeting or hearing within 60 days and require the agency to approve or deny the project at the meeting.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)  
 The initiative would also require a lead agency to make its permit decisions at the same time as its environmental review or determine that the project is exempt from environmental review. A responsible agency would be required to make permit decisions either 90 days from determining the application is complete or within one day of the lead agency approving the overall project, whichever is later. If an agency misses a deadline, the applicant would be authorized to grant more time or request a meeting or hearing that must be held within 45 days, where the agency must report its final decision. The initiative would authorize applicants to challenge adverse decisions in court.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)  
 

For court proceedings, the initiative would require that they be resolved within 270 days, with an optional court extension of 90 days.

Changes to environmental review

The initiative would change the environmental review process under CEQA for essential projects. It would limit the number of days an agency provides for public comment to 45 days for an environmental impact report (EIR). The initiative would also require a court order to extend the public comment period. Currently, state law sets a minimum number of days for the public comment period.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)[\[5\]](#cite_note-lao-5)

  
 The initiative would also allow essential project applicants to opt into a preliminary scoping process that allows the applicant to meet with the lead agency and provide information to discuss the project, potential environmental impacts, and alternatives to mitigate environmental impact. After participating in the scoping process, the applicant would be allowed to develop a single project alternative that may be considered during the preparation of the EIR. Currently, the lead agency is required to develop and consider a range of alternatives to mitigate environmental impact.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)[\[5\]](#cite_note-lao-5)  
 The initiative would require public agencies evaluating the project's environmental impact to base their evaluation on compliance with existing laws and on the "thresholds of significance" adopted or used by the agency at the time of application. Currently, agencies are authorized to use various impact thresholds throughout the review and application process, including project-specific thresholds.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)[\[5\]](#cite_note-lao-5)  
 

The initiative would make changes to the process by which applicants consult native tribes about potential projects. It would require applicants and lead agencies to consult with native tribes listed as federally recognized and not the state Native American Heritage Commission list. It would also require applicants to be screened by the lead agency and tribes that may experience effects to their cultural resources by the project. This would include developing ways to mitigate impacts that would be included as an enforceable requirement of the project. The initiative would also require essential project applicants to conduct a "good-faith" consultation" with tribes to be approved by a lead agency.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

Changes to judicial review

The initiative would increase the legal standard that courts use when reviewing challenges to a lead agency's authorization or environmental review. A challenge to the approval of an essential project would be "limited to whether the approval or authorization complies objective existing laws." The initiative would limit the *administrative record*, information used in CEQA cases, to documents the lead agency is required to make public, public comments and responses, and an applicant's response to the lead agency's questions about project compliance. Currently, the court can use independent judgment to determine an agency's compliance with CEQA.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)[\[5\]](#cite_note-lao-5)

  
 

The initiative would also limit how a court delays or stops a project. The initiative would not allow a court to rescind project approval if the court determines the agency's approval does not comply with CEQA. The initiative would allow the court to stop the part of the project that is not in compliance with CEQA or that poses a public safety risk, but only until it is corrected. The initiative would also prohibit other parts of the project from being challenged if they were not in the original court order. The initiative would also prohibit later challenges, from implementation to construction, if the agency's project approval was not challenged.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)[\[5\]](#cite_note-lao-5)

## Prediction markets

*See also: [Prediction markets](/Prediction_markets "Prediction markets")*

A prediction market is a platform where users buy and sell contracts tied to the outcome of future events. The price of a contract reflects the market's estimated probability of that outcome — a contract priced at 55 cents suggests the market estimates a 55 percent chance the event occurs. Volume reflects how actively a market is being traded.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) Unlike polls, which survey a sample of voters, prediction markets aggregate the financial stakes of individual bettors. A market with higher trading volume is generally considered more reliable than one with low volume, though prices can be influenced by large individual traders. 

This section displays the contract prices on the outcome of this election from Kalshi, one of several prediction market platforms. Ballotpedia displays prediction market data for informational purposes; these markets do not predict election outcomes with certainty.

## Background

### California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)

The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) was enacted in 1970. The law requires state and local government agencies to inform decision makers and the public about the potential environmental impacts of proposed projects and mitigate them as much as possible. CEQA applies to projects that need government approval or use public funds and could cause a physical change to the environment. The laws and rules that govern CEQA can be found in [Public Resources Code Section 21000](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=21000) and following, [California Code of Regulations, Title 14, Section 15000](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/california/14-CCR-15201#:~:text=California%20Code%20of%20Regulations%20Title%2014%2C%20§,and%20became%20operative%20on%20the%20same%20day.) and following, court rulings related to CEQA, and local CEQA procedures.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12)

## Key Findings

Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.

These are the key findings of the *Californians and their Government* survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:

*   **Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race.** Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
*   **Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label.** Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
*   **![Figure - Top state issues chosen by Californians](https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/survey-1026_key-findings_fig1.png)Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today.** Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
*   **![Figure - Top national issues chosen by Californians](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='385'%20height='149'%20viewBox='0%200%20385%20149'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today.** Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.

## November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures

Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.

**Gubernatorial Election.** California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our [July survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.

![Figure - Xavier Becerra leads Steve Hilton by a wide margin in the governor's race](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='652'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20652'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% [May survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% [October 2022 survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/)), and the 2018 general election (60% [October 2018 survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).

About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our [May survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in [October 2022](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in [October 2018](https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.

**House Races.** When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in [September](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), [July](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), [May](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and [February](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).

![Figure - A solid majority of California likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate if the 2026 election for the House of Representatives were held today](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='644'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20644'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in [May,](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in [September 2024](https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.

**Legislative Ballot Measures.** We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.

*   **Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs).** Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
*   **Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund).** Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
*   **Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns).** Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
*   **Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers).** Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
*   **Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services).** Forty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55 percent would vote no. In the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 43 percent said they would vote yes and 51 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 43 varies across partisan groups (28% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 41% independents) and age groups (30% 18 to 34; 37% 35 to 54; 50% 55 and older) and is below 50 percent across regions.

When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).

## Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot

In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).

After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).

![Figure - A majority of California likely voters would vote yes on Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes)](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='596'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20596'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.

A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.

Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).

Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.

![Figure - Fifty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote no on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax)](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='596'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20596'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.

A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.

Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.

Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.

## State of the State

Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.

When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.

Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since [June 2023](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.

![Figure - A majority of Californians think things in the state are generally going in the wrong direction](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='978'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20978'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.

With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in [February](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).

![Figure - Three in four feel their income is not keeping up with inflation](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='852'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20852'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since [October 2025](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.

Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last [October](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in [May](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.

When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
